say.text: A 34-year-old man is brought in after a kitchen fire. He has burns over the head and neck, the whole front of the trunk and the perineum.
Roughly what total body surface area is burnt?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Add the regions one at a time. Which regions carry a 9, which carry an 18, and which carries only a 1?
Yes. Head and neck is 9, the front of the trunk is 18, and the perineum is 1. Together that is 28%.
The same chart applies to any burnt region, and only partial and full thickness areas count toward the total.
That is not right. You gave the perineum a 9, which is the figure for the head or an arm. It is tempting because 9s and 18s are easy to swap in memory.
Why it fails: the perineum is 1%, so the total comes out 8 points too high. Right: head and neck 9, front of trunk 18, perineum 1, which is 28%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the figures in memory: 9 belongs to the head and each arm, and the perineum is 1.

say.text: That is not right. You gave the head an 18, which is the figure for the trunk or a leg. It is tempting because the head sits right beside the trunk.
Why it fails: the adult head and neck is 9%, so 37 overcounts by 9. Right: 9 + 18 + 1 = 28%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pin the figures: head and each arm 9, front and back of trunk 18, each leg 18, perineum 1.

say.text: Same chart, next region. In the adult rule of nines, how much does the perineum count?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about which region is the smallest on the chart. It is not the head, an arm, a leg or a side of the trunk.
Yes. The perineum is 1% on the adult chart, the smallest region you count.
The 9s are the head and each arm, and the 18s are the front and back of the trunk and each leg.
That is not right. You gave the perineum a 9, the figure for the head or an arm. It is tempting because 9 is the first figure most people learn.
Why it fails: the perineum is 1% in the adult chart, so a 9 overcounts by 8 points. Right: 1%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so swap this in memory: 9 is for the head and each arm, and the perineum is 1.

say.text: That is not right. You gave the perineum an 18, the figure for the trunk or a leg. It is tempting because the perineum sits at the lower edge of the trunk.
Why it fails: the perineum is 1%, and an 18 would overshoot by 17 points. Right: 1%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the 18s belong to the trunk front and back and to each leg, not to the perineum.

say.text: Now a 2-year-old girl, scalded over the whole head and both legs.
Which method should you use to estimate her TBSA?

choices.label: Adult rule of nines, as usual
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the adult chart was built for. Then ask whether a toddler's head and legs take the same share of the body.
Yes. The Lund and Browder chart gives each region a share that depends on age, so a child's large head and smaller legs are counted properly.
The adult rule of nines is the default only when the stem gives an adult, so age comes first.
That is not right. You applied the adult chart to a child. It is tempting because the rule of nines is the chart most learners memorise first.
Why it fails: in a child the head is about 18% and each leg about 14%, so adult figures overcount the legs and undercount the head. Use Lund and Browder.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the adult chart is not the default once the stem gives a child's age.

say.text: That is not quite right. The palm method suits small or patchy burns. It is tempting because it is quick at the bedside.
Why it fails: a palm is about 1% of TBSA, so it fits a small patch, not a broad scald over the head and legs. The age-based chart fits this case (K5).
The same 2-year-old, now a numbers question: the burn covers the whole head and one whole leg.
Using the child's figures, what is the TBSA?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Work out the head figure for a toddler, then the leg figure for a toddler. Are either of them the adult figure?
Yes. In a child the head is 18% and one leg is 14%, so 18 + 14 = 32%.
Age first, then the figures, and count only the partial and full thickness areas into the total.
That is not right. You kept the adult figures for the head and the leg. It is tempting because those are the figures already in memory, and the age in the stem is easy to skip.
Why it fails: an adult head is 9%, but a toddler's head is 18%, so the total comes out too low. Right: 18 + 14 = 32%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so age changes the figures before anything else is done.

say.text: That is not quite right. You counted the head with the child figure and the leg with the adult figure. It is tempting because the head is the region most people remember as large in a child.
Why it fails: both regions come from the same age-based chart, and mixing the two gives 36 here. Right: 18% for the head and 14% for one leg, so 32%.
Size the burn in two steps: pick the right chart for the patient's age, then count only the partial and full thickness areas.
A simple red, blanching area, the first-degree kind, is not counted toward TBSA for resuscitation.
Formal IV resuscitation is generally needed above 15% TBSA in adults and above 10% in children.
